**Incident:** worker-05d10803 (task-02249f0a, Durable project instruction contract, 4/6) reported its repo gate red solely because worker-c8c01fc6 (task-12e18265f7a, Runtime contract registry, 2/7) has `packages/contracts/src/runtime` mid-TDD.

**Root cause:** task-02249f0a DoD #4 requires "repository regression checks exit 0". Under epic rail 2 (single shared working directory, no worktrees) some other track is nearly always mid-edit, and a worker doing correct TDD is *supposed* to be red between its red and green steps. A repo-wide green gate is therefore unachievable-by-construction for most of any task's life. The DoD is not wrong in isolation — it is wrong under concurrency.

**Why this is worth logging separately:** the commit-index defect (`prop-734f1da5`) is about *writes* colliding. This one is about *verification scope* colliding. Same root — one tree, many workers — different surface. Expect a third variant: shared test fixtures or a shared barrel file.

**Handled:** told 05d10803 to continue on its focused gate (fully inside owned paths), defer the repo-wide check to completion where the DoD actually places it, and `report_blocked` naming the blocker rather than idle-wait if still red. Told c8c01fc6 not to truncate TDD to unblock anyone — just announce when contracts typecheck goes green. Neither is to touch the other's paths to make a gate pass.

**Not done, deliberately:** no DoD edit, no re-plan, no status flip. 05d10803 is 4/6 with local state worth preserving, and DoD authorship is not the governor's. Escalated the three options to the human — accept serialization, rescope the DoD to owned-path verification with repo-wide green at an integration gate, or cut concurrency.

⚠️ Governor procedure defect — logging against future-me, because I will hit this again.

**Unblocking is two calls, not one.**

`moe.report_blocked` sets *both* the task to BLOCKED and the worker to BLOCKED. `moe.set_task_status → WORKING` only clears the first. The worker stays BLOCKED and will not resume, no matter how runnable the task is.

I flipped task-02249f0a600247a6977949648ec64886 to WORKING at 12:41, told worker-05d10803 to hurry because the green window was closing, and then spent 11 minutes watching it not move. Pinged it twice asking what it was doing. It was doing exactly what it should: waiting to be released. The fix was `moe.unblock_worker { workerId, retryTask: true }`, which I did not call until 12:52.

**The tell was in front of me the whole time.** `moe.list_workers` showed `status: BLOCKED` with `isAlive: true` and `lastActivityAt` ticking. I read that as "quiet worker, do not panic, do not release" — correct doctrine, wrong diagnosis. Alive-and-BLOCKED is not the stale-worker pattern. It means the worker is parked waiting on a governor action.

**Discriminator for next time:**

| Signal | Means | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `status: CODING/READING_CONTEXT`, quiet, alive | mid-build, silent by design | wait — never release |
| `status: BLOCKED`, alive, task WORKING | waiting on you | `moe.unblock_worker` |
| `status: *`, `isAlive: false`, holds task | possible crash | ping, then human nod before release |

Cost: 11 minutes of a worker sitting idle on a task that was 6/6 complete and one command from DONE. No work lost, no corruption, nothing committed wrongly — pure latency, entirely mine.

Also worth recording: I pushed urgency on that worker at 12:41 predicting the repo-green window would close once `packages/store` work started. It did not close. 📋 Governance log — three findings since the last entry, plus the outbox split landed.

**1. Projection outbox core split 5 ways, human-approved.** architect-c4babdf9 blocked it as unplannable rather than producing a plan that faked atomicity. It was right: the owned subtrees could not reach the SQLite schema, `EventLedgerStore`'s commit seam, `SqliteEventStore` internals, `store/src/index.ts`, or `StoredEvent`'s missing schema version. Created five children with honest owned paths — step 1 (`task-50874e67`, schema + commit seam) is PLANNING, steps 2-5 in BACKLOG behind it. Parent parked in BACKLOG as a do-not-claim traceability shell; it refused `BLOCKED → ARCHIVED` so it needs a human to archive it later.

Left open deliberately: six downstream tasks list the parent as a hard dependency. Most want step 3 (transactional relay), not the whole chain. Told architects to repoint at the specific step when they plan those, rather than serializing the epic behind crash-hardening drills nobody uses.

**2. `pnpm-lock.yaml` is the fleet's only shared file — three tasks write it.** `@moe/core`, `@moe/skills`, and `@moe/runner` are all new-package scaffolds, so all three add a lockfile importer. Every other file across every WORKING task is disjoint.

The hazard is `pnpm install`, not the diff: it rewrites the whole lockfile from observed workspace state, so overlapping runs silently drop a sibling's importer or capture a half-created package. No merge conflict, no error — a lockfile that installs fine today and breaks a fresh checkout. Broadcast an announce-before-install protocol plus stage-only-your-own-importer to `#workers`.

**3. `@moe/core` ownership is narrower than reality, and it is already in flight.** The architects *did* coordinate the one-time scaffold correctly — Project goal lifecycle declares it, Identity session core does not re-scaffold. But two gaps remain: Identity has an undeclared hard dependency on that scaffold landing, and Identity cannot export its own API because the package root export is `src/index.ts`, which Project goal owns. Same failure shape as the outbox block, caught in flight instead of at planning. Asked architects to decide the export convention once and apply it to all future `packages/core/**` tasks.

**Method that found #2 and #3:** cross-referencing `affectedFiles` across every WORKING/BLOCKED task after each concurrency increase. Worth repeating — it caught the lockfile contention before anyone lost work, and it only works if plans declare files honestly. Both `@moe/core` tasks had "Owned paths" lines narrower than their actual `affectedFiles`; the plans were honest, the task descriptions were stale. Flagged that as a recurring defect.


|---|---|
| child proof UNKNOWN under record truth COMPLETE | `ok:true` COMPLETE |

`readRecord` checks top-level truth/coordinator/upstream co-presence only; `readItems` never enforces the disposition field matrix, canonical ordering, or identity uniqueness. **The decoder must re-derive the builder's invariants, not trust the digest** — self-consistent hostile bytes make `DIGEST_MISMATCH` unreachable as a defence.

**THE RULE, AS AMENDED — TWO ADMISSIBLE FORMS, output alone is neither:**
(a) A COMMAND THAT SURVIVES THE COMMIT and runs at the delivered tree — a committed test arm, a `grep -n`, a suite invocation. PREFERRED, always, when the claim is load-bearing for another row.
(b) THE PROBE'S FULL SOURCE INLINE in the record, so a grader can recreate, re-run, and delete it again.
A deleted probe's transcript is a LEAD, not evidence. It may found a filing (both of this morning's did, correctly) but it cannot discharge a DoD sentence.

**SCOPE, narrowed per QA and this is the important half:** the practice governs claims about behaviour THE ROW DOES NOT OWN — downstream callers, consumers, other packages, "nothing else needs X". Requiring a runnable command for every sentence about a row's own code turns completion records into transcripts and buries the one claim that mattered. All three of this morning's failures were downstream claims; that is the class worth policing.

**A WHOLE-FILE WRITE BUILT FROM A HEAD-BASED COPY IS A SILENT `git checkout` OF EVERY PEER'S UNCOMMITTED WORK IN THAT FILE.** No conflict, no warning, no porcelain evidence that anything was lost. It cost 157 lines at 13:24:30Z local on activation-ingress.test.ts: one lane added a 157-line block at 13:13Z; another rewrote the file from `git show HEAD:<path>`-shaped content, and `git diff --stat` afterwards read `25 insertions(+), 11 deletions(-)` — the second lane's edit ALONE.

**MY EDIT-ORDER RULING DID NOT COVER IT AND WAS NOT VIOLATED.** I had sequenced who edits first and that was honoured. **Whole-file regeneration discards concurrent work regardless of ordering** — which means ordering rules alone never protect a shared worktree. That is the governance lesson: I fixed the collision I could see and the loss came through a mechanism the fix did not address.

**PREVENTION (binding, posted to the fleet):** read the file from the WORKTREE immediately before writing, apply a TARGETED edit to that content, and never construct file content from `git show HEAD:<path>`, a stash, a template, or a from-scratch rewrite while a peer may hold uncommitted work there.

**DETECTION (because prevention will fail again):** after writing any shared file, `git diff --stat <path>` and compare insertions against what YOU added. **If the diff is smaller than your own edit, you overwrote someone.** That is precisely how it was caught here.

**RECOVERY THAT WORKED, worth copying:** the losing lane recovered its block from its own session record and RELOCATED it into a new file importing everything load-bearing rather than copying it — QA measured the relocation as real. Relocating beats re-fighting for a contended shared file.
